meta.blurb: Ben has a hot tip about one company, and he cannot explain why its price will keep rising. His friend Leila, with her first savings, asks a retired bank clerk instead. Mr Hale shows her low fees and plain funds.
meta.bible: Leila: a primary-school teacher aged twenty-nine, careful, curious, new to saving; she teaches at a school by the river and has taught for seven years. Ben: her cheerful friend who chases tips and hunches. Mr Hale: her retired bank clerk neighbour, patient, with a tidy garden and forty years in a bank; he gives Leila a small apple tree in a pot, which grows slowly through the book. Priya: Leila's colleague, who keeps her money in the bank and is saving for a flat. Mr Okoro: the deputy head, who likes property. Rosa, Kofi and Lena: three friends in an imagined bakery example. Brightwave: an imagined phone company, Ben's tip. Nina and Omar: two friends in an example about starting early. All money amounts are plain numbers with no currency. Leila has saved 5,000, her living costs are 1,000 a month, she owes 400 on a store card with a high interest rate, she clears it, keeps a 3,000 cushion and has 1,600 to invest, then adds 150 each month. Ben puts 800 into Brightwave and it falls by about a third. The examples (10,000 growing six percent a year for thirty years, a one percent yearly fee, Nina and Omar saving 100 a month) are imagined and are not promises. Key terms: share, dividend, diversification, fund, active fund, index, index fund, fee, bond, emergency fund, compounding, platform. Studies are described only in general, hedged terms; no invented figures. Tax rules differ by country. Voice: calm, kind, plain and practical, never promising returns. The final beat says this is general information and not financial advice.
chapters: A Ruler for the Whole Market

beats.scene: Leila sits at a kitchen table with a notebook, tea and a bank letter
beats.summary: Leila, a young teacher, has saved some money for the first time and wonders what to do with it.

beats.scene: Leila in a bright classroom, helping a small boy read a picture book
beats.summary: Her job is rewarding but not well paid, so saving has never been easy for her.

beats.scene: Leila's phone showing a small monthly transfer into a savings account
beats.summary: She saved by setting up a small monthly transfer and leaving the money alone for about two years.

beats.scene: A bank letter on the table with the number five thousand circled
beats.summary: The balance has reached 5,000, which makes her proud.

beats.scene: Leila reading a line in the letter about the low interest rate
beats.summary: The account pays very little interest, so her money is growing slowly.

beats.scene: A loaf of bread and an old shop receipt on a counter
beats.summary: Prices rise over the years, so money left idle buys a little less each year.

beats.scene: Priya in the staff room, holding a mug and shaking her head
beats.summary: Her colleague Priya says the bank is the safest place, and she never takes any risk.

beats.scene: Mr Okoro in the corridor, pointing at a newspaper advert for flats
beats.summary: The deputy head, Mr Okoro, says she should buy a flat and rent it out.

beats.scene: Leila's open notebook with a list of questions in neat handwriting
beats.summary: Everyone has advice, but nobody can explain it, so Leila writes down her own questions.

beats.scene: Leila's phone lighting up with a message from Ben on the kitchen table
beats.summary: Ben texts that he has the answer and invites her for coffee on Saturday.

beats.scene: Ben and Leila at a crowded café table with two cups
beats.summary: Ben leans across the table and tells her to buy shares.

beats.scene: Three friends making bread in a small bakery, with a sign on the door
beats.summary: Ben explains with an example: three friends need money to open a bakery.

beats.scene: Neighbours handing coins to the bakers in return for small paper certificates
beats.summary: The bakery sells small pieces of itself, called shares, to people who give it money.

beats.scene: A big modern company building with thousands of workers and a logo
beats.summary: A share is a small piece of ownership in a company, and large companies have millions of them.

beats.scene: A busy trading floor where people wave and shout, with a screen of numbers
beats.summary: A stock exchange is a marketplace where people buy and sell shares of large companies.

beats.scene: A baker handing small envelopes of money to smiling shareholders
beats.summary: Owners can earn when a company makes a profit and pays part of it out as a dividend.

beats.scene: A share price chart rising slowly while a baker sells more loaves
beats.summary: Owners can also earn when the company grows and the price of its shares goes up.

beats.scene: An empty bakery with a closed sign and a falling price chart
beats.summary: Nothing is guaranteed: a struggling company may pay no dividend and its share price can fall.

beats.scene: Ben scrolling through his phone proudly, showing only green numbers
beats.summary: Ben shows his winning shares but mentions none of the losers.

beats.scene: Leila looking thoughtfully at a list of thousands of company names
beats.summary: Leila understands shares now but wonders how anyone chooses which companies to buy.

beats.scene: Leila's phone showing a jagged share price line on a small screen
beats.summary: Leila watches a share price line on her phone and sees it jump up and down.

beats.scene: A newspaper headline about a company, with the price chart dropping beside it
beats.summary: Prices move on news, such as a good sales report or a problem at a factory.

beats.scene: A crowd of people running in different directions on a busy market square
beats.summary: Mood matters too: fear can make people sell and excitement can make them buy.

beats.scene: A fortune teller's crystal ball with a share chart inside
beats.summary: A price reflects guesses about the future, not only what the company earns today.

beats.scene: A smiling company chief with a trophy, while a share price chart falls
beats.summary: Even a great year can lead to a falling price if people had expected an even better one.

beats.scene: A row of confident experts on television pointing at different charts
beats.summary: Nobody can predict the market reliably, and experts often disagree with each other.

beats.scene: A restless crowd at a station, with a few people walking steadily away
beats.summary: In a short time prices are very hard to predict, but over long periods profits matter more.

beats.scene: Leila writing three company names on a sheet and ticking numbers each day
beats.summary: Leila tests this by pretending to buy three companies on paper and watching them for a week.

beats.scene: Leila's page of three lines going up, down and sideways with a puzzled expression
beats.summary: After a week her three pretend shares have moved in three different ways she did not expect.

beats.scene: Ben shaking his head with a sly smile and holding up his phone
beats.summary: Ben says that his tip is different, because it comes from somebody who really knows.

beats.scene: Ben whispering to Leila in a café, with a phone showing a company logo
beats.summary: The tip is Brightwave, a phone company, and the news came from a friend of a friend.

beats.scene: Leila holding a pen and a notebook, with Ben looking uncomfortable
beats.summary: Leila asks why the price will rise, and Ben says that everyone says so.

beats.scene: A notebook page listing questions about profit, rivals and price
beats.summary: She asks what the company makes, whether it earns a profit and who its rivals are.

beats.scene: Ben tapping a button on his phone to buy shares, grinning
beats.summary: Ben buys 800 worth of Brightwave anyway, and the price rises a little in the first week.

beats.scene: Leila lying awake at night with her phone beside the pillow
beats.summary: Leila feels the pull of missing out, and she wonders if she should join him.

beats.scene: A line written in a notebook, underlined twice, beside a cup of tea
beats.summary: She writes a rule: if she cannot explain why something will rise, she is only guessing.

beats.scene: A row of old shop signs, several with their windows boarded up
beats.summary: Many well-known companies of the past no longer exist, so even big names can fail.

beats.scene: A pile of 1,000 coins shrinking to a small stack of 100
beats.summary: A person who owns only one company's shares can lose most of what they put in.

beats.scene: A closed factory gate with a lock and a few workers walking away
beats.summary: If a company closes, its owners are usually paid last, so shares can end up worthless.

beats.scene: Leila crossing the street towards a neat house with a flowering front garden
beats.summary: Leila decides not to buy Brightwave, but wants a way that is not a bet, and goes to see Mr Hale.

beats.scene: Mr Hale trimming a hedge in a very tidy front garden
beats.summary: Mr Hale is trimming his hedge, and he invites Leila to sit down and talk.

beats.scene: Mr Hale in an old photograph, standing behind a bank counter
beats.summary: Mr Hale worked in a bank for forty years, and he has seen many money fashions come and go.

beats.scene: Leila explaining her problem with her notebook open on her knee
beats.summary: Leila tells him about Ben's tip, her notebook and her questions.

beats.scene: A farmer standing in a single big field of wheat under a stormy sky
beats.summary: Mr Hale describes a farmer with one field of wheat, whose whole year depends on one harvest.

beats.scene: A farmer with many small fields of wheat, beans, apples and sheep
beats.summary: A second farmer has many fields with different crops, so one bad harvest does not ruin her.

beats.scene: Mr Hale drawing a basket of many different company names on paper
beats.summary: Spreading money across many companies, industries and countries is called diversification.

beats.scene: A gardener covering seedlings with a cloth against frost, while a big storm gathers
beats.summary: Diversification does not remove risk; it lowers the risk of one company ruining you.

beats.scene: Ten stacks of coins, with one stack knocked over and ninety standing
beats.summary: If 1,000 is spread over a hundred companies and one fails completely, only 10 is lost.

beats.scene: Mr Hale handing Leila a small apple tree in a pot
beats.summary: Mr Hale gives Leila a small apple tree in a pot and says that growing things takes time.

beats.scene: Leila with the pot at the gate, Mr Hale pointing back at his house
beats.summary: Leila asks how she could own hundreds of companies with her small savings, and Mr Hale says that is what a fund is for.

beats.scene: A big wicker basket on a table filled with fruits and vegetables
beats.summary: Next day, Mr Hale draws a big basket and says a fund is a basket of many investments.

beats.scene: Neighbours putting coins into one big jar to buy seeds together
beats.summary: Many people put their money together, like neighbours who buy seeds in bulk.

beats.scene: A fund manager buying many shares for a shared pot of money
beats.summary: A company that runs the fund uses the pot to buy lots of investments, and each person owns a slice.

beats.scene: A slice of a basket whose contents rise and fall on a small chart
beats.summary: The value of each slice goes up and down with the value of the basket.

beats.scene: Three baskets on a table labelled shares, bonds and a mix
beats.summary: Funds can hold shares, other kinds of investment such as bonds, or a mixture of both.

beats.scene: Leila holding one coin and looking at a huge basket of company logos
beats.summary: Even a small amount of money can buy a slice of hundreds of companies through a fund.

beats.scene: A locked strongbox with a ledger and a stamp that says approved
beats.summary: In many countries funds must follow rules, and the money is kept apart from the manager's own.

beats.scene: Leila writing the word fund in her notebook with a question mark
beats.summary: Leila asks which fund to choose, and Mr Hale says there are two main kinds.

beats.scene: A team of experts around a table with charts and coffee, picking company names
beats.summary: In the first kind, a team of experts chooses what to buy; it is called an active fund.

beats.scene: Mr Hale pouring a second cup of tea and leaning back with a grin
beats.summary: Mr Hale pours more tea and says the second kind is quieter and more interesting.

beats.scene: A team of analysts at a whiteboard, drawing an arrow above a market line
beats.summary: An active fund tries to beat the market, which means doing better than the average of all companies.

beats.scene: Analysts in an office reading reports, with a map and calculator
beats.summary: The team reads reports, visits companies and builds spreadsheets, which sounds very impressive.

beats.scene: A payroll sheet showing salaries for analysts, offices and travel
beats.summary: The team of experts must be paid, and so must its offices, travel and research.

beats.scene: A tap dripping a small stream of coins from a jar
beats.summary: The fund pays for all this by taking a small percentage of the investors' money every year, called a fee.

beats.scene: A trader pressing buy and sell buttons many times, with charges on a screen
beats.summary: Active funds also buy and sell often, and every trade has costs that the investors pay.

beats.scene: Two price tags on two baskets, one marked higher than the other
beats.summary: Active funds charge higher yearly fees than simple funds do.

beats.scene: A glass jar slowly leaking water through a tiny hole, unnoticed
beats.summary: The fee is never sent as a bill, so you do not see it; the fund simply grows a little less.

beats.scene: A coin dropping into a bucket while another leaves through a tiny hole
beats.summary: Leila realises that an expert team needs to beat the market by at least its fee just to break even.

beats.scene: A runner with a heavy backpack racing another runner with none
beats.summary: Mr Hale says active funds run a race with a heavy bag on their backs, as fees slow them down.

beats.scene: Mr Hale folding his hands, with a second sheet of paper turned over
beats.summary: Leila asks whether the team can win every year, and Mr Hale suggests they look at the other kind of fund.

beats.scene: A huge shelf holding model buildings of every company in a country
beats.summary: Mr Hale says that the market means all the companies together, like a country's whole shopping street.

beats.scene: A giant ruler held next to a row of buildings of different heights
beats.summary: An index is a list of companies, used like a ruler to measure how the market is doing.

beats.scene: A list of the five hundred biggest companies pinned to a noticeboard
beats.summary: Some indexes list the biggest companies of a country, and others cover the whole world.

beats.scene: A newsreader on television with a number and a small green arrow
beats.summary: When the news says the index rose one percent, it means that the companies rose by about that much on average.

beats.scene: A tall giant and a tiny person standing on opposite sides of a see-saw
beats.summary: In many indexes bigger companies count for more, so a giant moves the number more than a tiny firm.

beats.scene: A blackboard showing a price times a number of shares equals value
beats.summary: A company's value is its share price times its number of shares, so a big company has a big value.

beats.scene: A group of people at a desk in an office, drawing up a list
beats.summary: An index is only a list and a rule, made by a company that publishes it; nobody can buy an index itself.

beats.scene: A machine copying a list of company names into a basket
beats.summary: An index fund buys every company on the list in the same proportions, so it copies the market.

beats.scene: A computer in a quiet room, with a finger on a list
beats.summary: Nobody has to pick shares, because a computer follows the list, and that is why index funds are called passive.

beats.scene: A list with a new name written in and an old name crossed out
beats.summary: Sometimes the list changes, and the index fund follows by buying or selling a few shares.

beats.scene: A small quiet office with a single computer and a sleeping cat
beats.summary: Index funds are cheap to run, because no team has to choose the shares.

beats.scene: A calm river beside a fast and noisy waterfall with foam
beats.summary: An index fund also needs little trading, since it changes only when the list changes, so its costs are low.

beats.scene: Mr Hale writing 10,000 and one percent on a sheet, and a result of 100
beats.summary: A yearly fee is a percentage: one percent of 10,000 is 100 each year.

beats.scene: Two bars, one tall and one very small, showing 100 and 10
beats.summary: A fee of a tenth of one percent on 10,000 is only 10, and the two funds differ a lot.

beats.scene: A hand reaching into a jar and taking a few coins out every year
beats.summary: The fee comes out of the fund every year, so it is really the investor's own money.

beats.scene: A young plant growing in a pot over thirty years, shown by thirty marks
beats.summary: In an imagined example, 10,000 growing six percent a year for thirty years becomes about 57,000.

beats.scene: Two plants of different heights after thirty years, with numbers 57,000 and 43,000
beats.summary: With a one percent yearly fee, the same money grows by five percent and ends at about 43,000.

beats.scene: A wide gap between two columns, labelled about 14,000
beats.summary: The gap of about 14,000 is nearly a quarter of the first total, and it is paid for the fee.

beats.scene: A taller plant of height 56,000 beside two shorter plants
beats.summary: With a fee of a tenth of one percent, the same example ends at about 56,000, close to the no-fee result.

beats.scene: Leila underlining a sentence in her notebook with a thick pen
beats.summary: Leila writes that fees are the one thing she can control, and the imagined numbers are not promises.

beats.scene: Leila raising a hand like a pupil in a classroom, in Mr Hale's garden
beats.summary: Leila asks whether the experts are not worth their higher fee, because surely a few of them win.

beats.scene: A stack of dusty research papers on a garden table
beats.summary: Many studies over long periods have found that most professional managers trail their index after fees.

beats.scene: A whole cake on a table with a few investors holding forks
beats.summary: Before costs, all investors together earn exactly the market's return, because together they own the market.

beats.scene: A seesaw with a winning investor high up and a losing investor low down
beats.summary: So when some investors beat the market, others must fall behind it by the same amount.

beats.scene: A cake losing slices to fees, and a plate marked below the market
beats.summary: Fees are taken from the investors, so after costs the average of all professionals must be below the market.

beats.scene: A single golden trophy shining among many grey ones in a cabinet
beats.summary: Some managers do beat the market in some years, but it is hard to know in advance which ones.

beats.scene: A thousand people flipping coins in a field, one cheering with ten heads
beats.summary: Skill and luck are hard to tell apart: among a thousand coin-flippers, about one will flip ten heads in a row.

beats.scene: A line of runners, with last year's winners at the back this year
beats.summary: Last year's winners are often not next year's winners, and past results do not promise the future.

beats.scene: A graveyard of small fund tombstones with a few bright living funds nearby
beats.summary: Funds that do badly are sometimes closed or merged, so the winners that remain can look better than the group really was.

beats.scene: Leila closing her notebook thoughtfully while the sun sets over the garden
beats.summary: Leila decides to look at index funds seriously, but wants to test the idea against Ben's way.

beats.scene: Ben's phone screen showing a red arrow and a steeply falling price line
beats.summary: Three weeks later Brightwave's price falls sharply after a poor sales report.

beats.scene: Ben's phone showing messages that say it is only temporary and wait
beats.summary: Ben texts that the fall is only temporary and that everyone must wait.

beats.scene: Ben sitting quietly in the park with his phone face down on the bench
beats.summary: Leila finds Ben at the park, quiet for once, and he cannot explain why the price fell.

beats.scene: A calculator showing 800 and then a smaller number, about 540
beats.summary: Ben's 800 is now worth about 540, a fall of about a third.

beats.scene: Ben holding a phone with two buttons: sell and wait, and hesitating
beats.summary: Ben cannot decide whether to sell and accept the loss, or wait and hope for a recovery.

beats.scene: Ben and Leila sitting together with a notebook between them
beats.summary: Leila asks Ben what he would do differently, and he says he would first want a real reason.

beats.scene: Mr Hale in his chair telling a story to Leila and Ben over tea
beats.summary: Mr Hale tells them that he once followed a tip himself and lost money, and learned from it.

beats.scene: Leila's list of fund types: country, world, small companies, bonds
beats.summary: Leila starts to look at index funds and finds that there are many kinds, such as ones for one country.

beats.scene: A globe covered with tiny dots, with a basket underneath
beats.summary: A whole-world index fund holds thousands of companies in many countries at once.

beats.scene: Four different baskets labelled small companies, bonds, one country and the world
beats.summary: Other index funds follow small companies or bonds, and each kind has its own risks.

beats.scene: A government building and a coin, with an arrow between them
beats.summary: A bond is a loan to a government or a company, and in return the borrower pays interest.

beats.scene: A calendar with yearly payments marked and a big payment at the end
beats.summary: If you lent 1,000 for ten years at three percent, you would receive 30 a year and get the 1,000 back.

beats.scene: A calm lake with a few small ripples beside a wavy sea
beats.summary: Bonds are usually steadier than shares, but they are not safe: a borrower can fail to pay.

beats.scene: A tree with deep roots and heavy fruit swaying in the wind
beats.summary: Over long periods, shares have often earned more than bonds, but not in every period, and it is not guaranteed.

beats.scene: A scale with growth on one side and a wave on the other
beats.summary: In investing, more possible growth usually comes with a bumpier ride, so risk and reward go together.

beats.scene: A pot with a plant labelled shares and a stone labelled bonds beside it
beats.summary: Many people mix the two: shares for growth and bonds for steadiness.

beats.scene: A young woman and an older man looking at two different pie charts
beats.summary: A young saver may choose more shares, while somebody near retirement may choose more bonds.

beats.scene: Mr Hale asking a question while Leila thinks with a pen in her hand
beats.summary: Mr Hale asks how she would feel if her money fell by a quarter, because nerves matter as well as age.

beats.scene: Leila writing a note by a pie chart that is mostly one colour
beats.summary: Leila decides that a mix with more shares than bonds suits her age and nerves, though it may suit nobody else.

beats.scene: A calendar with next spring circled and a small apple tree
beats.summary: Mr Hale says the mix is not fixed for life and she should look at it again when her life changes.

beats.scene: Mr Hale holding a calendar and asking a question across the garden table
beats.summary: Mr Hale asks when she will need the money, because the answer matters before she invests.

beats.scene: A shaky bridge to a house, with a calendar showing only five years left
beats.summary: Money needed within about five years should not be in shares, because prices can fall just when you must sell.

beats.scene: Priya holding a flat key and a savings book at her desk
beats.summary: Priya, who wants a flat in two years, is right to keep her deposit in a safe place, not in shares.

beats.scene: Three jars labelled now, soon and later on a kitchen shelf
beats.summary: Leila sorts her money into three jars: for now, for soon, and for later.

beats.scene: A jar marked emergency with three months of bills written on a label
beats.summary: Mr Hale says first she needs an emergency cushion of a few months of living costs in a safe account.

beats.scene: A broken washing machine, a flat tyre and a worrying letter
beats.summary: Emergencies come without warning, and without a cushion she might be forced to sell shares at a bad time.

beats.scene: Leila counting numbers on a calculator, with a note saying 3,000 kept safe
beats.summary: Leila counts: her cushion of three months is 3,000, and she has 5,000 in all.

beats.scene: A store card with a bright red percentage figure on the bill
beats.summary: Leila owes 400 on a store card with a very high interest rate, about twenty percent a year.

beats.scene: Leila cutting a card in half with scissors, and a small smile
beats.summary: Paying off the debt is a sure return: clearing 400 at twenty percent saves about 80 a year.

beats.scene: Leila's notebook with a clear sum: 5,000 minus 400 minus 3,000 equals 1,600
beats.summary: Leila pays off the card, keeps a 3,000 cushion, and has 1,600 left to invest.

beats.scene: Mr Hale unrolling a long paper chart on the garden table
beats.summary: Mr Hale shows her an old chart from the library: a market line that rises, falls and rises again.

beats.scene: A chart with deep valleys marked with dates, a finger pointing to one
beats.summary: Stock markets have fallen by a third or more several times, sometimes quickly.

beats.scene: A pile of 1,000 coins shrinking to a pile of about 670
beats.summary: After a fall of one third, 1,000 would become about 670.

beats.scene: A chart with a valley followed by a hill, and a sunrise behind it
beats.summary: So far, every big fall has been followed by a recovery, but the time it took has varied and nothing is guaranteed.

beats.scene: A staircase down by a third and a longer one up by half
beats.summary: After a fall of one third, the market must rise by half to get back, because the loss starts from a smaller number.

beats.scene: People walking calmly out of a building during a fire drill with a clipboard
beats.summary: Mr Hale says to decide in advance how she will behave when prices fall, like a fire drill.

beats.scene: A written rule on a fridge, held by a magnet, beside an apple tree
beats.summary: Leila writes her rule: she will not sell in a fall without waiting and writing down why.

beats.scene: A figure fleeing from a hill just before the chart turns upward
beats.summary: Selling in a panic turns a temporary fall into a permanent loss, and then you miss the recovery.

beats.scene: A calendar with a few days circled in different colours, close together
beats.summary: The best days in the market often come close to the worst days, so staying invested matters more than guessing the moment.

beats.scene: Leila walking home slowly under a streetlight, deep in thought
beats.summary: Leila realises that the skill in investing is patience, not prediction.

beats.scene: Leila holding a pile of coins and wondering, with a calendar behind her
beats.summary: Leila asks whether to invest her 1,600 all at once or in small steps over time.

beats.scene: A calendar page with the same sum written on every first day
beats.summary: Mr Hale says that investing the same amount every month removes the need to guess the right moment.

beats.scene: Three piles of fruit of different sizes on a table, marked with different prices
beats.summary: Mr Hale gives an example: with a fixed sum, you buy more units when the price is low and fewer when it is high.

beats.scene: A price line with a dip and arrows that buy at the dip
beats.summary: This does not guarantee a profit, and if prices only rise, investing everything at once would have done better.

beats.scene: A kitchen table with a budget sheet, a calculator and a cup of tea
beats.summary: Leila works out her budget and finds that she can invest 150 each month after her bills and a small treat.

beats.scene: A pay slip with an arrow pointing to savings before the shopping bags
beats.summary: Mr Hale says to pay yourself first, by moving the money on payday before there is time to spend it.

beats.scene: Leila on her laptop setting up a monthly payment into a new account
beats.summary: Leila sets up an automatic payment on payday into a separate account for investing.

beats.scene: A tap on a phone screen that says done, beside a sleeping Leila
beats.summary: Automation beats willpower, because the money moves without effort and she does not miss what she never sees.

beats.scene: Leila at a till choosing a small coffee and leaving a treat
beats.summary: Leila keeps a small budget for treats so that her plan feels fair and she will keep it up.

beats.scene: A pay slip with a larger number, and half the rise moving to savings
beats.summary: A rule for the future: when her pay rises, she will raise the amount she invests by half of the rise.

beats.scene: A fund basket with coins dropping into it from many trees
beats.summary: The companies inside a fund pay dividends, and the fund collects them on behalf of its owners.

beats.scene: Two doors, one marked cash and one marked reinvest, with coins at both
beats.summary: The fund can pay the dividends out as cash or reinvest them to buy more shares.

beats.scene: A tree dropping seeds that grow into more trees around it
beats.summary: Reinvesting buys more shares, which pay more dividends, so the money keeps working.

beats.scene: A small snowball at a hilltop and a huge one at the bottom
beats.summary: Compounding means earnings that themselves earn more, like a snowball that grows as it rolls.

beats.scene: A blackboard with 1,000, 1,100 and 1,210 in a growing column
beats.summary: At ten percent a year, 1,000 grows to 1,100, and then to 1,210, because the second year's gain is on more money.

beats.scene: A long line of numbers doubling slowly: 10,000, 20,000, 40,000, 57,000
beats.summary: At six percent, 10,000 doubles in about twelve years, then doubles again, and reaches about 57,000 in thirty years.

beats.scene: Two friends, Nina and Omar, on two different roads that reach the same city
beats.summary: Mr Hale tells a story of two friends, Nina and Omar, to show that time can matter more than the amount.

beats.scene: Nina at twenty-five putting coins in a jar, then stopping at thirty-five
beats.summary: Nina starts at twenty-five and saves 100 a month for ten years, then stops and lets the money grow.

beats.scene: Omar at thirty-five opening a jar and putting in coins every month
beats.summary: Omar waits until thirty-five and then saves 100 a month for thirty years, putting in 36,000.

beats.scene: Two jars of the same size at age sixty-five, with a clock behind
beats.summary: At sixty-five, both have about 100,000, because Nina's early start gave her money more time to grow.

beats.scene: A government tax office sign on a building beside a signpost to a form
beats.summary: Tax rules differ from country to country, so Leila must check the official rules for her own country.

B1B2: Leila is twenty-nine and teaches young children at a school by the river. This year she has saved some money for the first time, and she does not know what to do with it.
Leila loves her job, but a teacher's pay is modest. For years the money had gone as fast as it came, and she had never thought of herself as a saver.
Two years ago she set up a small transfer that moved money into a savings account each month. She tried not to think about it, and slowly the balance grew.
The letter from the bank shows a balance of 5,000. Leila reads the number three times, because she cannot quite believe that it is hers.
Further down the letter, Leila notices the interest rate. The bank pays her only a tiny amount each year for keeping her money safe.
Leila remembers that a loaf of bread cost much less when she was a child. Prices usually rise over the years, so money that just sits still buys a little less each year.
At school the next day, Leila asks her colleague Priya what she would do. Priya says the bank is the safest place, and that she will never risk her money on anything else.
In the corridor, the deputy head, Mr Okoro, tells her to buy a flat and rent it to tenants. Leila points out that her savings would hardly pay for the front door.
Everyone seems to have an opinion, yet nobody can explain why their advice is good. That evening Leila opens her notebook and writes down the questions she wants answered.
Just before bed, her friend Ben sends a cheerful message. He says that he knows exactly what she should do with her money, and he wants to tell her over coffee on Saturday.
On Saturday Ben arrives late, orders two coffees and leans across the table. He announces that the answer is simple: she should buy shares.
Ben takes a napkin and tells a little story. Three friends, Rosa, Kofi and Lena, want to open a bakery, but they do not have enough money for the ovens.
The friends decide to sell small pieces of the bakery to people who have spare money. Each piece is called a share, and the people who buy one become part owners.
So a share is simply a small piece of ownership in a company. A big company may divide itself into millions of shares, and each one belongs to somebody.
Shares of large companies are bought and sold on a stock exchange, which works like a big marketplace. Buyers and sellers meet there, and the price is simply the one they agree on.
When a company earns a profit, it may share some of it with its owners. This payment is called a dividend, and it is paid for each share that you hold.

There is a second way to earn money from owning a share, and it is the one people talk about most. If the company grows and does well, others will pay more for its shares, so the owners could sell at a profit.

Of course, nothing in the world of shares is ever guaranteed, as Ben admits when Leila asks. If the bakery does badly, it may pay no dividend at all, and its shares will probably be worth less than before.
Ben proudly shows her the shares that have gone up on his phone. Leila notices that he never mentions the ones that went down.
For the first time, Leila understands what a share is and how it can earn money. Her next question is a harder one: out of thousands of companies, how does anyone choose?
That evening Leila opens a share price chart on her phone and watches the line. It jumps up and down so often that she feels slightly seasick.
The next day she learns that prices react to news. A good sales report can lift a share price, while a problem at a factory can send it down within minutes.
Feelings move prices as well as plain facts, because markets are made of people. When people feel afraid they sell quickly, and when they feel excited they buy, even if nothing has really changed.
A share price is not only about what a company earns today. It also reflects what buyers guess the company will earn in the coming years.
Sometimes a company has a very good year, yet its share price falls. This happens when people had hoped for something even better.
On television, Leila finds experts who predict that prices will rise and others who say they will fall. They sound equally sure, and they cannot all be right.
Over a few days or weeks, nobody can say which way prices will go. Over many years, the profits that companies make tend to matter more than the mood of the moment.
To test the idea, Leila chooses three companies on paper and writes down their prices every day for a week. She has not spent a single coin, but she is learning a lot.
At the end of the week one company has gone up, one has gone down and one is almost unchanged. Leila realises that she could not have guessed which would do which.
When Leila tells Ben about her experiment, he only smiles. His tip is different, he says, because it comes from someone who really knows.
The tip is a phone company called Brightwave, and Ben heard about it from a friend of a friend. He says that the price is certain to rise, and he says it twice.
Leila asks Ben why the price will go up. He thinks for a moment and says that everyone he knows says it will.
She asks what the company actually makes, whether it earns a profit, and who its rivals are. Ben shrugs, because he has not looked at any of these things.
Ben buys 800 worth of Brightwave shares that same afternoon. In the first week the price rises a little, and he is delighted.
That night Leila lies awake, wondering if she should join him. She feels a small, uncomfortable pull, the fear of missing out on something good.
In the morning Leila writes a rule in her notebook and underlines it twice. If she cannot explain why an investment should grow, then she is only guessing.
Leila learns that many famous companies of the past no longer exist. Even a big name that everyone knows can lose its customers and disappear.
If a person owns only one company and it fails, the shares can lose most of their value. An investor who put in 1,000 might be left with 100.
When a company closes, the people it owes money to are normally paid first. Whatever remains goes to the owners, and often nothing remains at all.
Leila decides that she will not buy Brightwave, because she cannot explain it. She wants a way of investing that is not a bet, so she walks next door to see Mr Hale.
Mr Hale is trimming his hedge with great care when Leila arrives. He puts down his scissors, smiles, and invites her to sit on the bench by the roses.
Mr Hale worked in a bank for forty years before he retired. In that time he saw many fashions come and go, and he learned which ideas lasted.
Leila tells him about her savings, about Ben's tip and about all the advice she has received. She opens her notebook and reads out her questions.
Mr Hale asks her to imagine a farmer with only one field, full of wheat. If a storm or a drought ruins the crop, the farmer has nothing at all.
Now imagine a second farmer who has many fields, with wheat, beans, apples and sheep. If one crop fails, the others still feed her family and pay the bills.

Mr Hale explains that investors can do the same thing with money, by owning many companies in many industries and countries. The long word for doing this is diversification, and it simply means not putting everything in one place.
Mr Hale warns her that this does not remove risk completely. A storm can still hit every field at once, but one bad company can no longer ruin her.
Mr Hale picks up a pencil and gives her a simple example with numbers. If Leila spreads 1,000 evenly across a hundred companies and one of them fails completely, she loses only 10.
Before she leaves, Mr Hale gives her a small apple tree in a pot. He tells her that good things grow slowly, and that she must be patient.
At the gate, Leila asks how a person with small savings could possibly buy a hundred companies. Mr Hale smiles and says that this is exactly what a fund is for.
The next afternoon Mr Hale draws a large basket on a sheet of paper. A fund, he says, is a basket that holds many different investments at the same time.
Mr Hale says that many people put their money together into one big pot. It is like neighbours who club together to buy seeds, because a large order costs less and goes further.
A company runs the fund and uses the big pot to buy many investments. Each person who puts in money owns a slice of the whole basket.
The value of your slice depends on the value of everything in the basket. When the investments rise, your slice is worth more, and when they fall, it is worth less.
Some funds hold only shares, while others hold different kinds of investment called bonds. A few hold a mixture of both, so the basket can be built for different tastes.
With a fund, even a small amount of money buys a slice of hundreds of companies. Leila could never afford that much variety by buying the shares one at a time.
In many countries, funds must follow strict rules, and an official body watches them. The money is usually kept apart from the fund company's own money, which gives Leila some comfort.
Leila asks which fund she should choose, since there must be thousands of them. Mr Hale holds up two fingers and says that there are two main kinds.
In the first kind of fund, a team of experts chooses which shares to buy and sell. It is called an active fund, because the team is always busy making choices.
Mr Hale pours a second cup of tea and leans back in his chair. The other kind of fund is much quieter, he says, but first he wants to explain the active kind properly.
An active fund tries to beat the market, which means doing better than the average of all companies. That is a hard goal, and the team must be very good to reach it.
The team reads long reports, visits companies and builds huge spreadsheets. It all sounds very serious and impressive, and that is part of its appeal.
All of this work costs money, and somebody has to pay for it. The experts need salaries, the office needs rent, and the travel and research have to be paid for as well.
The fund pays for all this by taking a small percentage of the investors' money every year. This charge is called a fee, and it is taken whether the fund does well or badly.
Active funds also buy and sell shares very often, because the team keeps changing its mind. Each trade has costs, and in the end those costs are paid by the investors.
Because of all this work, active funds charge higher yearly fees than simple funds do. The difference may look small, but it is paid every single year.
The fee is never sent to you as a bill, so it is easy to forget. Your fund simply grows a little less than it otherwise would have done.
Leila works it out for herself, and she is pleased that the arithmetic is not difficult. The team must beat the market by more than its fee, or she would have done better with a cheaper basket.
Mr Hale smiles and says that an active fund runs a race with a heavy bag on its back. The fees weigh it down, and the team has to run much faster just to keep up.
Leila asks whether a team could win in every single year. Mr Hale says that they will come back to that, and turns over a fresh sheet of paper.
Mr Hale starts with a word that Leila hears every day: the market. In this sense it means all the companies of a country, or of the world, taken together.
To measure the market, people use an index, which is simply a list of companies. It works like a ruler that shows how the market is doing.
Some indexes list the biggest companies in one country, such as the largest five hundred. Others cover the whole world, or only small companies, or only one industry.
When the news says the index rose by one percent, the companies on the list rose by about that much on average. Some rose a lot more, and a few of them fell instead.
In many indexes, bigger companies count for more than small ones. A giant company moves the number more than a tiny firm does, because it has more weight.
A company's value in the market is its share price multiplied by its number of shares. If the price is 10 and there are a million shares, the value is ten million.
An index is only a list and a rule, published by a company that keeps it up to date. Nobody can buy the index itself, because it is not a thing.
An index fund buys every company on the list, in the same proportions as the index. In this way it copies the market instead of trying to beat it.
Nobody has to pick the shares, because the list does the picking. A computer follows it, and that is why index funds are sometimes called passive.
Sometimes the list changes, because a company grows, shrinks or leaves the list. The index fund follows these changes by buying or selling a few shares.
Because nobody has to choose the shares, an index fund needs no large team. That is the first reason why it is cheap to run.
The second reason is that an index fund trades very little. It only changes when the list changes, so it pays far fewer trading costs than an active fund.
Mr Hale explains that a yearly fee is a percentage of the money in the fund. One percent of 10,000 is 100, so that is the cost for one year.
Then he writes a much smaller fee: a tenth of one percent. On the same 10,000 that comes to only 10 a year, which is ten times cheaper.
The fee comes out of the fund every year, so it is really the investor's own money that pays for it. It never appears as a bill, and that makes it easy to ignore.
Mr Hale gives an imagined example, and he is careful to say that it is only imagined. If 10,000 grew by six percent a year for thirty years, with no fees at all, it would become about 57,000.
