The same collapse would be a catastrophe if all of her money had been in that one place.

As she rose to leave, Mr Hale disappeared into his shed and returned with a small apple tree planted in a pot. He told her to put it on her balcony and to remember that good things grow slowly, and that no amount of shouting will make an apple ripen faster. Leila laughed, held the pot against her chest like a baby, and promised faithfully to water it every single week.

At the gate, Leila turned round with the pot in her arms and asked the question that had been troubling her: how could a person with ordinary savings possibly buy a share in a hundred different companies? Mr Hale smiled as though he had been waiting all afternoon for exactly that question to arrive. That, he said, was precisely what a fund was for, and he asked her to come back tomorrow.

The next afternoon Mr Hale spread a large sheet of paper on his garden table and drew a basket on it, with a thick wicker handle. A fund, he said, is exactly that: a basket that holds a great many different investments at the same time. Leila decided that it was the first financial idea anyone had explained to her that she could actually picture in her mind.

The money, he explained, comes from many people who pool it together in one large pot, like neighbours who club together to order seeds for the whole street. A big order can buy things that no single neighbour could afford, and it usually costs less for each person. A fund works on exactly the same principle, but with shares and other investments instead of packets of seeds.

A company that specialises in running funds uses the combined money to buy a wide range of investments on behalf of everyone. Each person who contributes owns a slice of the whole basket, in proportion to what was paid in. Nobody has to choose, buy or sell anything alone, because the fund does the work in a single stroke.

The value of your slice depends entirely on the value of everything in the basket, so it moves whenever the investments inside it move. When the shares rise, your slice grows with them, and when they fall, it shrinks, with no cushion in between. A fund, Mr Hale emphasised, is not a safe deposit but a container for risk that is spread widely.

Some funds hold only shares, while others hold a different kind of investment called bonds, and a few hold a carefully chosen mixture of both. The basket, in other words, can be filled for different tastes and temperaments, and the label should always say what is inside. Leila resolved that she would always read the label carefully before she bought anything at all.

Through a fund, even a modest sum buys a slice of hundreds or even thousands of companies at once, which is a degree of variety that no small saver could ever assemble alone. Buying the shares one by one would cost a great deal in time, effort and charges. Leila began to understand why Mr Hale smiled when he said the word fund.

Mr Hale reminded her that in many countries funds must follow strict rules and are watched by an official regulator. The money in a fund is normally kept apart from the fund company's own money, so that a failing manager does not automatically take the investors down with it. He added that rules differ from place to place, and that she should always check where hers applied.

There must be thousands of funds in the world, Leila pointed out, and she wanted to know how a sensible person could choose between them. Mr Hale held up two fingers, like a conjuror about to reveal a card, and said that for her purposes there were really only two main kinds. One of them, he said, was far more popular with salesmen than with savers.

In the first kind of fund, a team of experts studies the companies, chooses which shares to buy and decides when to sell them. It is called an active fund, because the team is constantly busy, rearranging the basket in the hope of making it better. Mr Hale said that it sounded impressive, which was one of its selling points.

Mr Hale poured a second cup of tea for each of them and leaned back in his chair with the air of a man who has saved the best for later. The other kind of fund, he said, was a good deal quieter and a great deal less glamorous, but he wanted to explain the first kind properly before he moved on. Leila took out her notebook and wrote the word active at the top of a fresh page.

The aim of an active fund is to beat the market, which means earning more than the average of all the companies put together. That is a difficult and ambitious goal, because the average already includes the work of thousands of clever people. A team that merely matches the market has, in a sense, failed at the job it was hired to do.

The team reads long reports, interviews company chiefs, tours factories and builds spreadsheets of such size that they need a lorry to carry them. It all sounds extremely serious and thorough, and the brochures make the most of it. Mr Hale admitted that, in his younger days, he had been quite taken in by the performance.

All of this effort costs a great deal of money, and somebody, somewhere, has to pay for every bit of it. The experts need salaries, the offices need rent, the computers need electricity, and the flights to visit far-off factories need to be booked and charged for. Mr Hale pointed out, with a gentle smile, that the somebody is the person who owns the fund.

The fund pays its bills by taking a small percentage of its investors' money every year, and this charge is called a fee. It is collected whether the team has a brilliant year or a dreadful one, and it comes out of the basket before anybody sees the result. Leila thought it rather like a landlord who expects his rent to be paid in full whatever the weather happens to be.

Active funds also buy and sell shares very often, since the team is always acting on a new idea, a new report or a change of mood. Every trade carries a cost in commissions and in the gap between the buying and selling prices, and in the end those costs are paid by the investors. Constant activity, Mr Hale remarked, is not at all the same thing as steady progress, and it is often quite the opposite.

Because of all this work, active funds charge noticeably higher yearly fees than simple funds do, and the difference is paid year after year without a pause. Each percentage point may look trivial on the page, yet over a lifetime it has a way of becoming enormous. Leila underlined the word yearly in her notebook, because she suspected it was the important one.

The fee is never sent to the investor as a bill or collected at the door, so it is remarkably easy to forget. It is taken quietly from inside the fund, and all that the investor notices is that the price has grown a little less than it might have. Mr Hale compared it to a small leak in a bucket, unseen until the bucket is half empty.

Leila worked it out for herself, and she was rather pleased to find that the arithmetic was not difficult. To make a customer better off, the team must beat the market by at least the amount of the fee, and anything less leaves the customer poorer than a cheaper choice would have. Mr Hale nodded, and said that this was the whole argument in a nutshell.

Mr Hale smiled and said that an active fund runs the race with a heavy backpack strapped on, because its fees and trading costs weigh on every step. The team may be talented, and some of them are, but they must run noticeably faster than the market merely to arrive at the same moment. He did not say that no team could do it, only that it was a hard way to earn a living.

Leila asked whether any team could really win in every single year, since a few of them must be superb. Mr Hale said that they would come back to that excellent question, and then he turned over a fresh sheet of paper and began to draw a ruler. The other kind of fund, he said, started with a very different idea, and the idea was so simple that people kept forgetting to take it seriously.

Mr Hale began with a word that Leila heard on the news every day: the market. In this sense it means all the companies of a country, or of the whole world, considered together as one vast and bustling shopping street. When commentators declare that the market is up, they do not mean a single shop but the entire street.

To measure the market, people use an index, which is nothing more than a list of chosen companies together with a rule for counting them. It works like a ruler or a thermometer, since it tells you in a single number how the whole group is doing. The ruler does not make the market move, any more than a thermometer makes the weather.

Some indexes list the biggest companies in a single country, for instance the largest five hundred, and each country has its own famous examples. Others cover the whole world, or only small companies, or only a single industry such as energy or health. Anyone can look up exactly which companies a given index contains, and how large each one is.

When a newsreader announces that the index rose by one percent, she means that the companies on the list rose by about that much on average. Some of them rose by far more, a few fell, and the single number stands in for the whole crowd. It is a handy summary, much as an average mark summarises the results of a whole class, though it hides every individual story.

In many indexes, bigger companies count for more than small ones, so that a giant company moves the number far more than a tiny one does. It is like a seesaw on which the heaviest person decides which way the board tilts, however many light people sit on the other end. This sensible method is called weighting by size, and it mirrors the real market.

The value of a company in the market is found by multiplying its share price by its number of shares. If the price is 10 and there are a million shares, then the market values the company at ten million, and a larger company has a larger figure. In many indexes that figure alone decides how much each company counts towards the final number.

An index is only a list and a rule for counting it, published and kept up to date by a company whose business it is. Nobody can buy the index itself, since it is not an object but a measurement, just as you cannot buy the height of a mountain. What you can buy, however, is a fund that follows the list as faithfully as a shadow follows a walker.

An index fund buys every company on the list, in the same proportions as the index itself, so that its basket looks like a small copy of the whole market. It does not try to be clever and it does not try to beat anybody. Its only ambition is to deliver what the market delivers, minus a small fee.

Nobody in an index fund has to pick shares, because the list does all the picking, and a computer simply follows it. This is why such funds are sometimes called passive, and the word is not an insult but a description of their method. Mr Hale thought that being boring, in this particular case, was a very fine quality, and he said it with obvious pleasure.

From time to time the list changes, because a company grows, shrinks, merges with another or leaves the list altogether. The index fund follows each change by buying or selling a few shares, with no meeting and no debate. Leila noticed that this made it a sort of living photograph of the market rather than a bet on any one corner of it.

Because nobody has to choose the shares, an index fund needs no army of analysts, no glossy brochures and no expensive travel. A small team and a good computer system can run a fund that holds thousands of companies. That is the first of the two reasons why index funds are so cheap to run.

The second reason is that an index fund hardly trades at all, for it buys or sells only when the list changes or when new money arrives. An active fund, forever acting on new ideas, pays trading costs on every move, and the investors bear the bill. Quiet funds are cheap funds, Mr Hale told her with a satisfied nod, and in all his years at the bank he had never seen an exception.

Mr Hale took out his pencil again and explained that a yearly fee is always a percentage of the money in the fund. One percent of 10,000 is 100, so a fund with a fee of one percent takes 100 from that pot in a single year. A hundred sounded modest to Leila, and she said so, but Mr Hale only raised a finger and asked her to wait for the next part of the sum.

Then he wrote down a much smaller fee, a tenth of one percent, and applied it to the same 10,000. The answer was only 10 a year, which is ten times lower than the first figure, and exactly the sort of fee that many index funds charge. Leila began to see that the numbers which look tiny on a page are the ones that need the most attention.

The fee, Mr Hale reminded her, comes out of the fund every single year, which means that it is really the investor's own money that pays for it. It never arrives as a bill or a reminder, and for exactly that reason it is easy to ignore. What the investor does not see, the investor rarely questions, and the companies that collect the fees understand this very well.

Mr Hale then offered an imagined example, and he stressed the word imagined, since nobody can promise a rate of growth. If 10,000 grew by six percent every year for thirty years, with no fees whatever, it would become about 57,000. It is a pleasing figure, and yet it was only the beginning of his point.

Now suppose that a fee of one percent is taken every year, so that the money grows by five percent instead of six. After thirty years the same 10,000 has become only about 43,000, and the investor has done nothing wrong at all. Leila whistled quietly, for the difference seemed far too large to be the work of a single percent.

The gap between the two results was about 14,000, which is nearly a quarter of the larger total, and it had gone entirely to pay the fee. The effect is so large because each year's fee also removes everything that money would have earned for the rest of the thirty years. A fee of one percent, Leila saw, is not small at all when it is paid for decades.

Mr Hale repeated the calculation with the lower fee of a tenth of one percent, and the answer after thirty years was about 56,000. That is not far below the figure for a world without any fees, and it is about 13,000 better than the result for the dearer fund. The saver's reward for choosing cheaply, she noted, was entirely legal and required no talent at all.

Leila wrote in her notebook that she could not control the price of anything in the market, but she could certainly control the fees she paid. Mr Hale reminded her that his numbers were only imagined, and that nobody knows what the future growth of any market will be. The fee, however, is a certain cost, and it is paid whether the market rises or falls.

Leila raised her hand like one of her own pupils, and Mr Hale pretended to look stern and invited her to speak. Surely, she said, some of the experts must be skilful enough to earn their higher fee, otherwise nobody would pay it. It was a fair question, and he said that the evidence deserved a careful answer.

Mr Hale said that many studies, carried out in different countries over long periods, have reached a similar conclusion. Most professional fund managers have earned less than a plain index fund once their fees and costs were taken off, though the exact results depend on the place and the years. He cautioned that studies are not laws of nature, but that the pattern has been remarkably consistent.

There is a simple reason for this, and Mr Hale explained it with a cake. All the investors together own the whole market, so together they must earn exactly what the market earns, before anyone has paid a single fee. Nobody, however clever, can eat more than the whole cake, and every extra slice that one person takes must be taken from somebody else.

It follows that for every investor who beats the market by a certain amount, somebody else must trail it by the same amount. The whole business is like a seesaw, in which one end can only rise if the other falls. Once the fees are paid, the average professional must therefore do a little worse than the market itself.

Fees and trading costs leave the cake and never return to it, since they are paid to the people who run the system. So after costs, the average professional can only earn a little less than the market, and the gap equals the total of all the fees. It is arithmetic rather than opinion, and Leila found that reassuring, because arithmetic does not depend on anybody's mood or on anybody's sales pitch.

Mr Hale did not deny that some managers beat the market in some years, and a few of them manage it for quite a long time. The difficulty is that nobody knows in advance which ones they will be, since the winners cannot be recognised until they have already won. By then, the money that followed them has often arrived too late to share in the success that attracted it in the first place.

Skill and luck are surprisingly hard to tell apart, and Mr Hale showed her why with a coin. If a thousand people each flip a coin ten times, about one of them will throw ten heads in a row, purely by chance. That person might be hailed as a genius, although he has done nothing except be lucky.

In the same way, last year's winning funds are often not the winners of the following year, and some of them end up near the bottom of the table. A good record in the past, Mr Hale said, is a poor promise about the future, however loudly the advertisements trumpet it. This is why the small print always warns that past results are not a guide.

Mr Hale added a subtle point, which was that funds that do badly are sometimes closed or merged into other funds, and then disappear from the record. The survivors that remain look better than the whole group really was, because the failures have quietly vanished from the table. A list of only the winners, he warned, is always a flattering mirror, and a sensible person should ask where the others have gone.

Leila closed her notebook, thanked Mr Hale for the tea and the lesson, and walked home through the evening light with her mind turning. The idea of the index fund made sense to her, but she was a teacher and wanted to see the evidence unfold before she trusted it. She would watch what happened to Ben's tip over the coming weeks, and only then would she decide what to do with her own money.

Three weeks later Brightwave published a sales report that was far weaker than anybody had hoped, and its share price began to slide at once. By the end of the week it had lost almost a third of its value, and the confident messages from Ben had stopped completely. The silence, Leila thought, was far more eloquent than any of the boasts that had come before it.

At last, on the Thursday evening, Ben sent a short message in which every word seemed to have been chosen with care. The fall was only temporary, he wrote, and the clever thing to do was simply to wait for the price to recover. It was impossible to tell whether he was trying to reassure Leila or himself.

Leila found Ben on a bench in the park, with his phone lying face down beside him, which was most unlike him. When she gently asked him why the price had fallen, he admitted that he could not explain that either, any more than he had been able to explain why it would rise. He had been equally sure, and equally in the dark, in both cases, and he finally seemed to see the joke.

Ben had put in 800 only a month before, and the shares were now worth about 540, which meant that a third of his money had melted away. He tried to smile and to joke about it, but it was money that he had meant to spend on a holiday with his sister. Leila felt sorry for him, and she did not say a word about her notebook.

Ben could not decide whether to sell and accept the loss or to wait and hope that the price would climb back. Both choices felt miserable, and, as he confessed, neither was based on anything he really understood about the company. Leila did not tell him what to do, because the honest answer was that nobody could know.

Leila did not say that she had warned him, because it would have helped nobody, and she asked instead what he would do differently next time. After a long and thoughtful pause, Ben said that he would demand a genuine reason before he committed a single coin, and that a friend of a friend was no reason at all. It was, Leila reflected, quite the most sensible remark that she had ever heard him make in all their years of friendship.

When Leila told Mr Hale what had happened, he laughed kindly and said that everybody has been Ben at least once, himself included. In his twenties he had followed a tip from a colleague with a very loud voice, lost a good part of a year's savings and spent months feeling foolish. It was, he said, the cheapest and most useful lesson of his whole career.

That evening Leila began to study index funds in earnest, with the notebook and a pot of tea beside her laptop. There were many kinds, she found, and some followed only the biggest companies of a single country, while others followed a particular industry or region. It was a little like discovering that the word basket covers everything from a shopping bag to a picnic hamper.

A whole-world index fund, she discovered, holds thousands of companies in dozens of different countries at the same time, from giant banks to small makers of machines. It was diversification carried about as far as it can go, and a single failure of a company or even a country would barely register. This, she thought, was Mr Hale's farm of many fields, multiplied a thousand times and spread over the whole of the world.

Other index funds followed only small companies, or only bonds, or only certain industries, and the list seemed to grow with every click. Each of them had its own level of risk and its own fee, and a label that sounded attractive might not mean what she expected. She would have to read before she decided, and she was happy to do it.

Mr Hale explained that a bond is simply a loan, made by an investor to a government or a company that needs the money. In return the borrower pays interest at regular times, and then gives the original sum back on an agreed date. Whoever holds a bond is, in effect, playing the part of a bank, and is paid for lending rather than for owning.

Mr Hale gave an example with numbers that she could easily hold in her head, and he used his pencil again. If you lent 1,000 to a borrower for ten years at three percent, you would receive 30 every year, and at the end the borrower would hand back the 1,000. The arrangement is predictable, he said, and that predictability is the whole point of the bond.

Bonds usually bob up and down much less than shares do, and for that reason they are often called the steadier part of a portfolio. They are not free of danger, however, because a borrower can fail to pay what it owes, and bond prices also change when interest rates move. Steadier, Mr Hale said, does not mean safe, and a careful saver should never confuse the two words.

Over long periods of time, shares have often earned more than bonds, which is the reason why many savers hold plenty of them. This has not been true in every period, however, and nobody can promise that the future will follow the pattern of the past. Higher growth was a possibility, Leila noted in the margin, but it was never a guarantee, and she underlined the word never.

Here was the great bargain of investing, Mr Hale said: the chance of more growth usually arrives together with a bumpier ride. Risk and reward travel together, and anyone who promises a high return with no risk at all is either mistaken or selling something. Leila copied the sentence into her notebook, and she drew a box around it.

Many people, Mr Hale told her, hold a mixture of the two, using the shares for growth and the bonds for steadiness. The balance between them is a personal choice, and there is no single correct recipe that suits everybody. It is a little like deciding how much salt to put into soup, only with higher stakes.

The right mixture depends on the age and the needs of the saver, Mr Hale said. A young person with decades ahead may hold more shares and wait out the storms, while somebody close to retirement may prefer more bonds because the money will soon be needed. He admitted that his own savings, at his age, now leaned heavily towards the quiet kind.

Then Mr Hale asked a harder question, and it had nothing to do with arithmetic. How would she feel, he wanted to know, if her savings fell by a quarter in a few months, and could she sleep and go on as before? Nerves matter as much as age, he said, because a plan that you abandon in a panic is worth nothing.

Leila thought carefully and decided that a mixture with more shares than bonds would suit her age and her nerves. She wrote down her reasons in full, and she added that it was a choice for her alone and might not be right for anybody else. Writing down the reasons, she suspected, would matter a great deal on a bad day.

Mr Hale reminded her that the mixture is not fixed for life, and that it should be looked at again whenever something important changes. A new job, a move, a child or simply the passing of the years might all be reasons for a change. A plan, he said, is a living thing, a bit like her apple tree.

Before they went a step further, Mr Hale asked a question that she had not yet considered, and which he said was more important than any fund. When would she need this money, he asked, and for what purpose in her life? The answer, he explained, decides almost everything that comes after it, from the kind of fund to the amount of risk.

Money that will be needed within about five years, Mr Hale said, should not be placed in shares at all, however attractive the market may look. Prices can fall just at the moment when you are forced to sell, and a short deadline leaves no time to wait for them to recover. The nearer the date, the quieter and safer the home that the money needs, and the less it should depend on the mood of the market.

Leila thought at once of Priya, who hoped to buy a flat within two years and who had been so firm about keeping her money in the bank. For a goal as near as that, Mr Hale said, Priya was perfectly right, because shares could be down on the very day the deposit was due. It was an odd sort of victory for the staff room, and Leila decided to tell Priya so the very next morning, with her compliments.

Leila began to think of her money as three jars on a shelf: one for now, one for soon and one for much later. Only the third jar, the one for a distant future such as her retirement, was suitable for shares, since only that one could wait out a long storm. The other two jars, which held the money for the coming weeks and the coming years, needed much calmer homes where nothing could shrink on a bad day.

Before she bought a single share, Mr Hale said, she needed an emergency fund, which is a cushion of a few months of living costs kept in a safe account. The money must be easy to reach at short notice and impossible to lose, and its job is to be there when life goes wrong. Leila's own costs came to about 1,000 a month, so for her three months meant 3,000, which she could picture quite clearly in a single pile.

Emergencies arrive without any warning, in the form of a broken boiler, a sudden car repair, an illness or a job that disappears. Without a cushion, Leila might be forced to sell her shares on the very day when prices were lowest, turning a temporary dip into a lasting loss. A cushion, Mr Hale said, buys the freedom to be patient, and patience was exactly what a long-term investor needs the most.

Leila worked it out on her calculator, with her tongue between her teeth as she did when marking exercise books. Three months of costs came to 3,000, and she had 5,000 altogether, so there was a surplus, but it was smaller than she had hoped. Then she remembered something that she had been avoiding for months, and she knew at once that the surplus was going to shrink a little further.

Then Leila remembered the store card that she had used in a moment of weakness, for a coat that she did not need. She still owed 400 on it, and the card charged a high rate of interest, about twenty percent a year. It was quietly working against her every day, and she had been ignoring it.

Mr Hale said that paying off an expensive debt is one of the few sure returns in the whole world of money. Clearing 400 at twenty percent saves about 80 a year, with no risk and no waiting, which is a gain that no share in any market can promise. Costly debt, he advised, should usually be cleared before anything at all is invested, though each person's situation is a little different.

Leila paid off the store card that same evening, and she moved 3,000 into a separate account for emergencies. After that, she had exactly 1,600 left for the long term, and it felt like a smaller sum than before and a far more solid one. Her plan finally had a floor under it, and she slept better than she had for weeks.

Mr Hale unrolled a long paper chart that he had copied from a library book, covering the value of a whole market over many decades. The line climbed, shuddered, collapsed, recovered and climbed again, like a path through hilly country. It was, he said, a map of every storm that the market had survived.

Mr Hale pointed to the deepest valleys on the chart and said that stock markets have fallen by a third or more several times over the past hundred years or so. Some of those falls happened slowly over many months, and others happened with frightening speed, within a few weeks. Anyone who invests in shares, he warned, should expect to meet a storm of that size at least once.

Leila did the sum on her calculator, as she always did, and the result was sobering to look at. If the market fell by a third, 1,000 would shrink to about 670, and she would see that loss on her screen each time she looked at it. It is one thing to read about a storm in a book, and quite another to stand in the rain.

So far, Mr Hale said, every great fall has been followed by a recovery, and Leila felt her shoulders relax a little. He cautioned her at once that the recoveries took different lengths of time, from months to several years, and that no law of nature guarantees that the pattern will go on. Patience, he said, is a requirement of this way of investing and not a prize, and it is the price that must be paid for the possible reward.

After a fall of one third, Mr Hale showed her, the market must rise by one half just to get back to where it began, because the rise starts from a smaller number. Falling is easier than climbing, and a large loss is harder to repair than a small one. This is one more reason why surviving the bad times is as important as enjoying the good ones.

Mr Hale advised her to decide in advance how she would behave when prices fell, and not to wait for the moment itself. It is rather like a fire drill, in which everybody walks calmly to the door because they have rehearsed it, whereas an unprepared crowd would run and trample one another. Decisions made in fear, he said, are rarely wise ones, and a calm rehearsal on a quiet day is worth a great deal on a frightening one.

Leila took a blank card and wrote her own rule in clear letters: if prices fell, she would not sell in a hurry, and before she touched anything she would wait a month and write down her reasons. She pinned the card to the fridge, where she would see it every single morning. The next storm, she hoped, would find her ready, and the card would remind her of how clearly she had thought on a calm day.

Selling in a panic, Mr Hale explained, turns a temporary fall into a permanent loss, because the investor locks in the lower price. Worse still, the same investor then misses the recovery, which often begins when the news is at its most terrifying. It is one of the most costly mistakes in all of investing, and it is made by thousands of people in every downturn.

Mr Hale added that the best days in a market often come close to the worst days, so that anybody who jumps out in fear is likely to be absent when the rebound arrives. Missing only a handful of those days, he said, can reduce the result over many years by a surprising amount. Staying invested therefore matters far more than trying to guess the right moment, which nobody, however clever, has ever managed to do reliably.

Walking home beneath the streetlights, Leila turned over everything that she had heard that evening. The skill that mattered, she decided, was not prediction but patience, and unlike prediction, patience was something that she could practise every day. It was a rather unfashionable conclusion in a world that adores quick answers and bold forecasts, but she found that it comforted her deeply.

Leila asked a question that had been bothering her for days, and it was one that every new investor eventually asks. Should she put her 1,600 into the market all at once, or feed it in gradually over several months, in case prices fell the day after she bought? Mr Hale said that both were reasonable, and that the real secret lay somewhere else.

The real secret, said Mr Hale, was to invest the same amount of money at the same time every month, whatever the headlines might say. In that way she would never have to guess the right moment, which nobody can do reliably, and she would never be tempted to wait for a better day. Habit, Leila reflected, was a far steadier master than hope, and it was certainly a great deal cheaper than a lifetime of second-guessing.

Mr Hale gave her a tiny example with imagined prices, written out in a neat column. If she invested 100 each month, and the price of a unit was 10, then 5, then 10, she would buy ten units, then twenty, then ten again. In all she would have spent 300 and bought forty units, so her average cost per unit would be less than the average of the prices.

Mr Hale was honest about the limits of the method, and Leila admired him for it. It does not guarantee a profit, and if prices happened to rise all the time, then putting everything in at the start would have done better. What it offers is not the best possible result but a calm and ordinary way to take part, which is often worth more.

Leila sat down with her budget and went through it line by line, from rent and bills to bus fares and her weekly coffee. When everything had been paid, and a small allowance for treats had been set aside, she found that she could invest 150 each month without feeling squeezed. A plan that causes pain, Mr Hale had said, is a plan that gets abandoned.

Mr Hale urged her to pay herself first, by moving the money on the very day that her pay arrived, before there was any opportunity to squander it. Most people, he observed, save whatever happens to be left at the end of the month, and in most months nothing at all remains. Leila had already discovered this truth, from the transfer that had quietly built her first 5,000.

That evening she opened her banking app and set up an automatic payment that would move 150 into a separate account on each payday. The account was meant for investing and nothing else, and she gave it a plain name so that she would not be tempted to borrow from it. It took only five minutes to arrange, and yet it would go on working in the background for years and years to come.

Automation, Mr Hale told her, beats willpower every time, because it spares you the daily argument with yourself. The money moves without effort, and nobody misses a sum that they never see sitting in the current account. Her future self, Leila thought, was getting a small gift every month, and she had not had to lift a finger.

Leila deliberately kept a small amount in her budget for treats, because a plan that feels like a punishment rarely lasts for long. The point of the exercise was not to turn herself into a miser but to build a habit that she could comfortably keep for decades. Mr Hale agreed that a life without any pleasure is a poor reward for a lifetime of saving.

Leila added a rule for the future, and she was rather proud of it. Whenever her pay rose, she would raise the amount she invested by half of the increase, and she would keep the other half to spend on a better life today. In this way her savings could grow steadily without her ever feeling that she had lost something.

Leila learned that the companies inside a fund pay dividends from their profits, just as the bakery had done in Ben's story. The fund collects all of these payments on behalf of its owners, the people who hold the slices, and then it must decide what to do with all of the money that has come in. There were two choices open to it, and the choice that was made would matter a great deal over the coming years.

A fund can either pay the dividends out to its owners as cash, or it can reinvest them automatically in more shares and let them grow inside the basket. Some funds are built to do the first and some the second, and the label on the fund explains which sort it is. For a saver who does not need an income yet, the second kind is often the natural choice.

When dividends are reinvested, they buy a few more shares, and those new shares in turn pay dividends of their own. The money is therefore never idle, and it works away quietly in the background like seeds that grow into trees which then scatter seeds. Leila looked across at her pot with its single young apple tree, and she smiled at the thought of a very small forest of her own.

Mr Hale gave the process its proper name, which is compounding, and he said it as though it were a small miracle. It means that the earnings of an investment begin to earn something themselves, so the growth feeds upon its own results, like a snowball that gathers more snow with every turn. The effect is gentle and almost invisible at the start, and yet astonishing towards the end, which is why patience is the only price of admission.

Mr Hale gave a simple example with an imagined growth of ten percent a year. After one year 1,000 becomes 1,100, and after the second it becomes 1,210, because the second year's gain of 110 is earned on a larger sum than the first year's gain of 100. The difference of 10 seems tiny, but it repeats every year and keeps on growing, until it overtakes everything that came before it.

Returning to the imagined 10,000 growing at six percent, Mr Hale showed that it doubles in about twelve years, and then doubles again over the next twelve. By thirty years it has reached about 57,000, which means that most of the growth comes in the final years of the story. The longer the money is left alone, the faster the line climbs, and the more generous the later years become towards the patient.

To show how important time is, Mr Hale told a story about two imagined friends, Nina and Omar, who both saved 100 a month and who both earned six percent a year. The only difference between them was the moment that they began, and the story shows how large a difference that moment can make. Leila put her cup down, folded her hands in her lap like one of her own pupils, and listened with the closest attention she could manage.

Nina began at twenty-five and saved 100 every month for just ten years, putting in a total of 12,000. Then she stopped adding anything, and from the age of thirty-five onwards she simply left her money alone to grow. She did nothing at all for the next thirty years except wait, and the patient waiting was the whole of her strategy.

Omar, who was busy enjoying himself, waited until he was thirty-five before he began, and then he saved 100 every month for thirty years. In all he put in 36,000, which is three times as much as Nina had contributed. He thought it was a very fair deal, and for his effort it was.

At sixty-five, said Mr Hale, the two friends would each have about 100,000, even though Nina had paid in only a third as much. Her early start had given her money far more time to compound, so that the passing of the years had accomplished what her wages never could. The lesson, he added, was not to lament a late start but to begin at once, because starting at any age is wiser than waiting for some perfect and elusive moment.

Mr Hale reminded Leila that tax rules differ from country to country, and that they also change from time to time. He could not tell her what applied in her own case, so she would have to consult the official rules, or an adviser, before she acted. This book, he said, was only a general conversation over tea, and not a substitute for reading the rules or asking a qualified adviser.

Some countries offer special accounts in which investments are taxed lightly or not at all, and these accounts can make a large difference over the years. Leila went to her government's own website rather than to a stranger's blog, and she read the rules slowly, taking notes as though she were preparing a lesson. The official source, she had decided, was the only one worth trusting for something so important.

To choose a fund, Mr Hale suggested, a sensible person asks four questions, and he counted them off on his fingers. The first and most basic is what the fund follows, whether it is a single country, the whole world or some narrower slice of the market. A fund whose name is attractive but whose contents are vague, he said, should always be left on the shelf.

The second question concerns money, and it is the one that she now understood best: what does the fund cost every year? She should look for the yearly fee, which is printed in the fund's documents, and compare it with those of similar funds that follow similar lists. A difference of a fraction of one percent, as she had learned, can be worth thousands.

The third question is how wide the fund is, in other words how many companies and how many countries it holds. A fund that contains thousands of companies from dozens of countries spreads the risk a long way, whereas one that contains only a few may be nothing more than a clever bet. Wide, Leila wrote in the margin, usually means safer from the failure of any single piece.

The last question concerns who runs the fund, and whether it is approved and watched by an official regulator in her own country. A long record, a sensible size and a clear explanation of what the fund does are all good signs, while vague promises are bad ones. Leila decided that she would be suspicious of any fund that was harder to understand than a bakery.

Every fund publishes a short sheet of key information, and Leila discovered that reading it was much less frightening than she had expected. It set out the costs, the risks and the list of what the fund followed, and she ticked off each point against her four questions. For the first time, the world of investing felt like something she could inspect for herself.

To buy a fund she needed a platform, which is a regulated company through which ordinary savers can buy and hold funds. Leila listed three of them side by side and compared their account charges, their trading fees and the clarity of their websites. She noticed that the loudest advertisement was not the one with the lowest cost, which was becoming a familiar pattern.

To open an account, Leila had to prove who she was, which is a rule that exists to protect savers and to prevent crime. She photographed her passport, filled in a long form and linked the new account to her own bank, and the platform promised to review her details within a few days. Waiting for the answer, she thought, was an excellent rehearsal for the patience that investing would demand of her in the years to come.

Mr Hale gave her one last warning, and he gave it very seriously, because he had seen too many people hurt. Scammers send messages that promise guaranteed returns or urgent chances, and no honest company can promise a certain profit, so she should always check that a business appears on the official register. A tempting offer that arrives out of the blue, he said, deserves nothing but suspicion.

A few days later the platform sent a message to say that her account was ready, and Leila read it standing up in the kitchen. She moved some money in from her bank, which took a day to arrive, and she felt a flutter of excitement that she tried hard to hide from herself. It was real now, and the careful days of questions and notes in her notebook had given way to actual money in an actual account.

She chose a wide, low-cost index fund that followed thousands of companies all around the world, and she checked it against each of her four questions. It cost very little each year, it was run by a reputable company, and its information sheet was clear enough to be understood by a patient child. She ticked the last box on her card with a pleasing sense of completion.

She had decided to begin with a modest first amount of 400, and to add the rest of her money over the following months. Her finger hovered over the buy button for what felt like an hour, and her heart beat slightly faster than usual. Fear and excitement, she noticed with some surprise, feel remarkably alike from the inside, and it is only afterwards that one learns which was which.

At last she pressed the button, and her finger trembled a little as it came down. Nothing dramatic followed, for there were no trumpets and no flashing lights, only a quiet message that confirmed the purchase. Becoming an investor, it seemed, was mostly a matter of clicking once and then having the patience to leave it alone.

Leila opened the list of everything that the fund held, and she scrolled down it with growing amazement. She now owned a tiny slice of thousands of companies in many countries, and she recognised some of the names from the shops she visited and the phone in her pocket. For so small a sum as 400, it was a truly remarkable amount of variety, and the thought of it made her smile.

When Leila told Mr Hale what she had done, he raised his teacup in a solemn toast, like a man proposing the health of an old friend. She had done the hardest part, he said, which was to begin, and everything after it would consist mostly of doing nothing. He said the last words with relish, because to him they were a form of art.

Ben telephoned that evening and burst out laughing when he heard what she had done. Was that all, he wanted to know, because he could not see how a purchase with no excitement and no secret could possibly be worthwhile. Leila replied, quite calmly, that she had been looking for an investment and not for entertainment.

For the first three days Leila checked the price of her fund every few hours, and each small movement made her feel pleased or worried in turn. None of it meant anything at all, since a change of a fraction of one percent is only the noise of an ordinary day. Her mood was being governed by a number that had no business governing it.

Leila made herself a new rule, and she wrote it in the first square of each month on her calendar. She would look at her fund only once a month, on the same day that she looked at her apple tree to see whether it had grown. Both of them, she told herself, were things that cannot be hurried by staring.

When the first monthly check came round, the fund had dropped a little, and the red number made her stomach turn over for a moment. She remembered the card on the fridge, took a long breath, closed the screen and did nothing at all. It was her first small test, and she had passed it by the simple method of refusing to act.

Mr Hale reminded her that the fund's own yearly fee is not the only cost that an investor may meet. There may also be a fee charged by the platform, a charge each time shares are bought or sold, and a cost for changing from one currency into another. Each is small on its own, but costs of every kind have a way of joining forces.

Leila built a table with a row for every cost that she would pay, and she added them up to find the total yearly cost of her plan. Then she did the same for a second platform, and the difference, although small in a single year, was enough to make her change her mind. She had learned that a careful comparison is the cheapest hour of work in the whole business.

She also read the small print of her platform, which was long and dull and written in the language of lawyers. She wanted to know exactly when each charge applied and what she could do to avoid the unnecessary ones, such as paying more often than she needed. A little boredom now, she reasoned, could save a great deal of money later.

Ben, who traded on his hunches several times a week, finally sat down and added up what his trades had cost him. Every single trade had carried a small charge, and the total over a few months was a good deal larger than he had imagined. Leila did not say a word, but she let him see her notebook with the table of her own costs.

Every day there was a new headline about a coming boom or a looming crash, and every one of them was delivered with total confidence. Such forecasts rarely help a long-term investor, Mr Hale said, because nobody predicts the market well and nobody does it often. The news exists to hold attention, and that is a different task from helping people to grow their savings.

A forecaster who happens to be right once is praised for years, while the many forecasters who were wrong are quietly forgotten. This makes it extremely hard to tell the lucky from the wise, since only the successes are ever put on display. Leila decided that she would treat every confident prediction with the same polite scepticism.

New fashions in investing arrive every year, each of them dressed up as a revolution and each promising to make the old ways obsolete. Most fade within a few seasons, and many leave behind a trail of disappointed buyers. Leila kept her core plan simple and boring on purpose, and she came to regard that boredom as a precious asset.

Mr Hale said that some people like to keep a small amount, perhaps a tenth of their savings, to spend on their hunches and enthusiasms. The point of such a fun jar, he explained, is that the main plan remains untouched, however badly the game may go. Leila did not need one herself, but she thought that Ben very much did.

Mr Hale was quite clear that an index fund gives the average result of the market, and that an average is not a guarantee. It can fall, sometimes sharply, and nothing in its past promises what it will do in its future. He would rather have her know the risks than imagine a safety that does not exist.

At her second monthly check the fund had risen a little, and Leila felt a warm glow of satisfaction that she had to remind herself to distrust. One good month proved no more than one bad month had done, and she was careful to feel neither too clever nor too foolish. Being merely average at low cost, she realised, was no small thing, and it was a good deal more than most people ever manage to achieve.

The months passed in a steady rhythm, and Leila hardly noticed them go by, which was exactly what her plan had been designed to achieve. On her balcony the apple tree put out new green leaves, and her fund rose and fell as the market rose and fell, without once troubling her sleep. Boredom, it turned out, was a surprisingly comfortable place to live, and she had never been so free from worry about money.

Once a year, in the spring, Leila sat down at the kitchen table to review her whole plan, with a cup of tea and her old notebook. It was twelve months since she had bought her first slice of the fund, and the same bank letter that had started everything lay beside her. A little pile of savings had become a small, sensible plan, and she could hardly believe that it had begun with a single confused evening.

At the review she raised the amount that she saved each month, because her pay had risen and she had promised herself half of the increase. She would change the plan itself only if something large altered in her own life, such as a new home, a child or a different job. Her own mood and the mood of the market, she decided, were not good reasons to change anything.

She also checked whether the mixture of shares and bonds had drifted far from her original plan, as it will when one part grows faster than the other. Because the shares had grown a little more quickly, she directed some of her new money towards the bonds to bring the balance back into line. Mr Hale had called it tidying the garden, and she rather liked the phrase.

Ben arrived at her door with two coffees and a sheepish grin, and he confessed that his tips had given him very mixed results. One of them had risen, another had fallen, and Brightwave had climbed back only a little of what it had lost. Taken together, he said, he had worked very hard and ended up almost exactly where he had begun.

Then Ben surprised her by announcing that he had opened an index fund of his own, in a wide and low-cost version that was remarkably like hers. He kept only a small amount for his hunches, which he now called his entertainment budget, and he declared that it made his life much less tiring. Leila laughed until she had to put her coffee down, and she felt very proud of him.

Ben asked her to explain the whole idea again, from the beginning, and Leila did so in her own words and without once looking at her notes. She drew the basket and the ruler on a sheet of paper, and she saw with some astonishment how much she had learned in a single year. A person who cannot explain an idea has not understood it, she had once told herself, and now she could.

Priya, who had heard about it in the staff room, asked to read Leila's notes, and Leila was glad to lend them. She shared what she had learned but was careful not to tell anybody what to do with their own money, because every person's situation is different. Teaching, she thought, was something she had always known how to do, and now she was doing it with a new subject.

Leila wrote her whole plan on a single page, in her neat teacher's handwriting, and pinned it to the fridge beside the old card about falling prices. It said: save first, hold a wide index fund, add a little every month, ignore the noise, and stay patient. There was nothing on the page that a ten-year-old could not have understood, and that, she felt, was its great strength.

The index fund way is simple and patient, and it asks for little more than low costs, wide ownership, regular saving and the courage to do nothing for a very long time. It is not magic and it offers no guarantees, and this book is general information, not financial advice, so anyone with a particular situation should ask a qualified adviser. Leila, watching her small tree grow, felt that she had finally planted something, and that time would do the rest.
